newsitem.title: USA: House passes fisheries bill, sends to Clinton.
newsitem.headline: House passes fisheries bill, sends to Clinton.

text.p: The House Friday passed a bill to protect the nation's declining fisheries, clearing the legislation for President Clinton's signature.

The House voted 384 to 30 for the measure, which the White House has said it generally supported as well. But in debate some Democrats complained they were forced to accept the Senate's somewhat weaker version of the bill intended to clamp down on wasteful fishing practices and protect fish habitat.

With the congressional session drawing to a close, other congressmen said the bill was such a drastic improvement from the current law that they felt they could not wait another year or two to pass a stronger bill. The House approved the Senate bill to avoid the time-consuming process of working out differences between the two versions.

While conservation groups generally preferred the House bill, they endorsed the final bill reforming the 20-year-old Magnuson Fisheries Act. The act was written to make U.S. fisheries off-limits to foreign fishing operations but it spurred a rush for domestic exploitation of fishing resources.

With over-fishing and the wasteful practice of netting large amounts of non-commercial aquatic life, then dumping it overboard dead or dying, many fisheries are on the brink of collapse. In the North Pacific alone, as much as 750 million pounds of fish is dumped overboard annually and Gulf shrimpers dump nearly that much.
The Commerce Department has said restoring fisheries would have a $25 billion economic impact and create 300,000 jobs.

While the House passed its original version of the bill a year ago, the measure stalled in the Senate in a dispute between Alaska and Washington state lawmakers over access to North Pacific fisheries.

After the Senate unanimously passed its bill this month, Alaska Republican Sen. Ted Stevens warned that if the new rules did not work to curb wasteful practices of factory fishing trawlers in the North Pacific, he would push a bill to ban the trawlers. Trawlers operate mostly out of Washington.
